label: Nutrition & Dietary Pattern
description: How your overall eating pattern — not any single food — shapes cellular aging, from telomere length to mitochondrial function and gut microbiota balance.
webSearchHint: peer-reviewed nutrition and telomere/aging research from PubMed, NIH, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, or major dietetics journals
emphasis: Draw on the full document, which covers four distinct dietary patterns (Mediterranean, Plant-Based, Okinawan, DASH), each linked to 3-4 distinct cellular mechanisms (telomere preservation, membrane protection, mitochondrial support, gut microbiota, autophagy, AMPK, mTOR, FOXO3, NF-kB, mitophagy). Do not default to 'Mediterranean diet + fiber' every time — that is the single most overused pattern in this library. Check what mechanism and dietary pattern were used in the user's recent history (if provided) and deliberately rotate to a different pattern/mechanism than last time. If several sub-sources support the same swap, pick ONE concrete food/action as the actual instruction and list the rest as swaps rather than presenting a menu.

label: Gut Microbiome & Metabolic Byproducts
description: The bacteria in your gut ferment fiber into compounds that influence inflammation, metabolism, and how well your intestinal barrier holds up as you age.
webSearchHint: peer-reviewed microbiome, short-chain fatty acid, or gut-barrier research from PubMed/NIH, Nature Microbiology, or Cell Host & Microbe
emphasis: Draw on the full document, which covers three distinct mechanisms: SCFA production (butyrate/propionate/acetate — each with its own producing bacteria and effects), chronic inflammation reduction (inflammaging, cytokine reduction, immune modulation, LPS/endotoxin translocation), and gut barrier integrity (permeability, mucus layer, Akkermansia). Rotate across these three mechanisms rather than defaulting to 'add fiber' every time — a barrier-integrity or inflammation-reduction angle (e.g. polyphenol-rich foods for Akkermansia, or prebiotic foods like onions/garlic/leeks for cytokine reduction) is just as well-supported as SCFA/fiber and produces a genuinely different, more specific action. Do not stack the 22-food comparison, the 25g/day study, and generic 'increase gradually' guidance into one unsignposted claim — keep it clear which finding is which if more than one is used.

label: Sense of Purpose & Social Connection
sourceLabel: Sense of Purpose & Longevity research ladder
description: A strong sense of purpose is one of the most consistently replicated predictors of longer life across large population studies — this is the best-evidenced topic in the library.
webSearchHint: peer-reviewed psychology/epidemiology research on purpose, meaning, or ikigai from PubMed, NIH, or major university behavioral-science departments
emphasis: This source has 8 distinct sections (all-cause mortality, cardiovascular, stroke, cognitive decline, physical function, biological mechanisms, behavioral mechanisms, modifiability) — treat them as 8 different angles, not one. Vary the actual action across turns: a reflection/journaling prompt, a message to another person, a values-linked activity choice, a preventive-care reminder tied to the Kim/Strecher/Ryff healthcare-use finding, or a stress-buffering action tied to the loneliness/stress meta-analyses are all equally valid and should not collapse into 'send someone a message' every single time. Check the user's recent history (if provided) and do not repeat the same action type two turns running. This is the best-evidenced topic in the library — do not pad with material from other topics' sources.

label: Sleep Quality & Circadian Health
sourceLabel: Sense of Purpose & Longevity research ladder (sleep-adjacent findings only)
description: Sleep quality and circadian regulation are foundational to recovery — though this topic currently borrows adjacent findings rather than drawing on a dedicated sleep-science source.
webSearchHint: peer-reviewed sleep and circadian-rhythm research from the NIH National Center on Sleep Disorders Research, PubMed, Harvard Medical School's Division of Sleep Medicine, or the Sleep Foundation's cited primary research
emphasis: The static library only has two adult sleep citations (the 825-adult purpose/sleep-quality cohort, and the Health & Retirement Study 16%-lower-risk finding) in section 6. This is genuinely thin — this is exactly the topic where live web search should do real work: look specifically for adult circadian-rhythm and sleep-hygiene research (light exposure timing, consistent sleep/wake times, temperature, caffeine half-life) from the credible domains above to give this topic real depth instead of reusing the same two purpose-adjacent citations every time. Do not use the early-childhood-development document for this topic under any circumstances — it is a pediatric source and citing it for an adult user is a population mismatch, not valid support for an adult sleep habit.
knownLimitation: This topic has no dedicated adult sleep-science source in the static library — it borrows two sleep-adjacent findings from the Purpose document and is expected to lean on live web search (restricted to credible domains) for topic-specific depth.

label: Physical Activity & Movement
sourceLabel: Sense of Purpose & Longevity research ladder (movement-adjacent findings only)
description: Physical activity is one of the best-established levers for healthy aging — this topic focuses on small, sustainable ways to move more, not workout prescriptions.
webSearchHint: peer-reviewed exercise-science and physical-activity research from PubMed, NIH, the CDC's Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans (adult sections only), or the American College of Sports Medicine
emphasis: The static library only has one adult movement citation (the Hooker & Masters 2016 accelerometer-based purpose/movement study) in section 7. Like Sleep, this is a genuinely thin topic where live web search should add real, adult-specific exercise-science depth (e.g. specific step-count or activity-minute thresholds with their associated mortality/longevity risk reduction) rather than reusing the same purpose-linked citation every time. Do not use the early-childhood-development document (its CDC guidance is written for children, not adults) — that population mismatch was a real failure caught earlier in this project.
knownLimitation: This topic has no dedicated adult exercise-science source in the static library — it borrows one behavioral finding from the Purpose document and is expected to lean on live web search (restricted to credible domains) for topic-specific depth.

label: Metabolic & Cardiovascular Risk
sourceLabel: DASH Diet research (Nutrition document, DASH section only)
description: Blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar share the same dietary levers — this topic focuses on the DASH-diet mechanisms behind all three.
webSearchHint: peer-reviewed cardiometabolic research from PubMed, NIH, the American Heart Association's published studies, or the DASH diet's original NEJM/Harvard trials
emphasis: Use the DASH Diet section of the document, which covers 5 distinct mechanisms (eNOS/endothelial optimization, insulin sensitivity, and others) — rotate across which one anchors the action rather than defaulting to the same eNOS-fiber framing every time; blood-pressure, lipid, and glucose framing are three genuinely different angles even on the same DASH foods. Do not pull from the Mediterranean, Plant-Based, or Okinawan sections — those belong to the Nutrition topic and using them here would blur the two topics into duplicates.

label: Micronutrient & Vitamin Status
description: Vitamin and mineral status — and how genetics can shift individual needs — plays a quiet but measurable role in aging and chronic disease risk.
webSearchHint: peer-reviewed nutrient-metabolism research from PubMed, NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, or major endocrinology/nutrition journals
emphasis: This source is written in directive clinical dosing language ('if you carry variant X, take Y'). You must never repeat that framing. Prefer the general-population, whole-food-first findings (e.g. the 390,124-person null result on daily multivitamins) as the default, and treat genotype-linked passages only as a prompt to mention that genetic variation in nutrient needs exists and is worth discussing with a clinician who can test for it — never as a personalized dose. The source covers at least 7 distinct nutrients (Vitamin D, Folate/MTHFR, Omega-3/APOE4, Magnesium, Vitamin B12, Selenium, Vitamin K2) plus the multivitamin null result — rotate across these rather than defaulting to the same one turn after turn; check the user's recent history if provided. If the user's profile lists one or more 'Genetic Variants' (e.g. MTHFR, VDR, HFE, TRPM6, FADS1/ELOVL2, PEMT, BCMO1, GPX1, zinc transporter), check whether this source has a matching passage and, if so, work it into the Why using the same non-dosing, research-population framing — never as a personalized instruction. If none of the reported variants match anything in this source, or the user reported none, proceed with the general-population guidance only; do not ask the user for genetic data they have not provided.

label: Cognitive Health & Neuroprotection
description: Brain aging is shaped by both psychosocial factors like purpose and specific nutrients like B12, folate, and omega-3 fatty acids.
webSearchHint: peer-reviewed cognitive-aging or dementia-prevention research from PubMed, NIH National Institute on Aging, or the Alzheimer's Association's cited primary research
emphasis: Check BOTH source files before answering, and default to the MICRONUTRIENT document's B12/folate/omega-3 cognitive-aging passages as the primary mechanism for this topic — not the purpose document's Alzheimer's/dementia section. A real quality failure was caught earlier in this project where this topic simply reused the Purpose topic's citation and reflection-writing action almost verbatim; do not repeat that. Only fall back to the purpose/cognition evidence if the micronutrient angle has already been used in the user's recent history (if provided) or genuinely does not apply. If the user's profile reports the APOE4 allele or a FADS1/ELOVL2 variant specifically, the micronutrient document's omega-3/APOE cognitive passages are written for exactly this case and should be checked first, using the same non-dosing, research-population framing as the Micronutrient topic.

label: Energy & Mitochondrial Function
sourceLabel: Mitochondrial-health research (Nutrition document, Mediterranean & Okinawan mechanism sections)
description: Mitochondrial health depends on specific dietary compounds — polyphenols, healthy fats, fermentable fiber — that support cellular energy production.
webSearchHint: peer-reviewed mitochondrial biology or cellular-energy research from PubMed, NIH, or journals like Cell Metabolism and Mitochondrion
emphasis: Use the mitochondrial-health, AMPK-activation, and mitophagy-stimulation sections within the Mediterranean and Okinawan parts of the document — three distinct mechanisms, not one. Rotate across them (mitochondrial biogenesis via polyphenols, AMPK activation via specific compounds, mitophagy via curcumin/polyphenols) rather than defaulting to the same 'olive oil and fatty fish' framing every time. State clearly when a cited finding is from pre-clinical/animal research rather than human studies, and carry that caveat through into the sentence that states the claim, not just as an appended disclaimer.

label: Weight Management & Body Composition
description: Weight management here is framed around appetite-hormone signaling from fiber fermentation — not calorie counting.
webSearchHint: peer-reviewed research on satiety hormones, GLP-1/PYY signaling, or body-composition from PubMed, NIH, or major endocrinology journals
emphasis: Use the propionate/GLP-1/PYY satiety-signaling section of the gut microbiome document. Justify recommendations through this appetite-hormone mechanism specifically, not the general SCFA/inflammation framing used for the Gut Microbiome topic. This is the narrowest single-mechanism topic in the library (only one real angle in the static source) — this is a good candidate for live web search to add a second, genuinely different angle (e.g. protein's effect on satiety hormones, or resistance-training's effect on body composition) so this topic doesn't feel identical to Gut Microbiome every time.
